work.title: 志玄安樂經 (Book of Profound and Mysterious Peace and Joy)
work.edition: Machine translation (claude-opus-5-5, Patristica, 2026-11-13) of: Chinese Wikisource, «志玄安樂經», revision 2009893 (2020-12-26); reading text of the manuscript formerly in Li Shengduo's collection, published in Kyōu Shooku's Tonkō hikyū (Osaka); □ marks the manuscript's gaps. Its beginning is lost. Listed in the Zunjing among the books Jingjing translated.

paragraphs.text: When these perfect words had been heard, the Supreme [?]—the Messiah—was in the Hall of Pure Emptiness with all the [?] assembly. They surrounded him on every side and stood in reverent attendance. [?] Simon rose from among the assembly, folded his arms [?], and said: "We people are deluded and firmly [?]. By what means [?] may living beings be saved and protected [?]?"

The Messiah answered: "Excellent, [?]! You seek to share in the supreme Law. Sit down again and compose your spirit [?]. All kinds of beings possess peace and joy. [?] nature follows [?]. It is like the moon in water: because the water is muddy, no reflection appears. It is like fire in the grass: because the grass is wet, no light is seen. Living beings who are sunk and buried are just the same.

"Simon! Whoever cultivates the supreme Way must first rid himself of agitating desire. Without agitating desire, there is no seeking and no striving. Without seeking and striving, one can become clear and pure. Being clear and pure, one can awaken and realize. Awakening and realizing, one illuminates everything and reaches every realm. Illuminating everything and reaching every realm is the condition for peace and joy.

"Simon! Take my own person as an example: I have wondrous features and an extraordinary will, and the ten marks I bear are called the Four Attainments. Yet of the Four Attainments I have never been aware in myself, and the ten marks I have never seen in myself. It is only to teach people that I give them provisional names. In the true source itself there is in fact no knowing or seeing. Why is this? If there were knowing and seeing, there would be a self. Because there is a self, one harbors thoughts of life. Because one harbors thoughts of life, one seeks and strives. Seeking and striving is what is called agitating desire. Whoever has agitating desire cannot yet escape suffering and affliction, much less attain peace and joy. Therefore I say: be without desire and without striving, leave all defiling realms, and enter every pure source. Leaving defilement, one can become pure, and so become like empty space, sending forth the light of wisdom that can illuminate all things. Because it illuminates all things, it is called the Way of Peace and Joy.

"Further, Simon: I am in all the heavens and on all the earths, whether in the realm of spirits or in the human world, among beings of the same kind and of different kinds, sentient and insentient. All who have good karmic conditions I protect and uphold; all who suffer evil retribution I rescue and deliver. Yet in this saving and protecting, there is truly nothing that is heard of. It is like empty space, free of any appearance of merit or virtue. Why is this? If there were merit and virtue, there would be fame. If there were fame, one would set oneself apart. If one set oneself apart, one would be the same as ordinary minds. Those who share the ordinary mind are not yet free from pride and boasting, much less able to attain peace and joy and perfect understanding. Therefore I say: those without virtue and without fame let their compassion flow freely and bring all living beings to deliverance. Relying on spiritual power, they awaken to the true and the real. Awakening to the true and the real is the Way of Peace and Joy.

"Again, Simon: through the faculty of the eye I see forms without hindrance; through the faculty of the ear I hear sounds without hindrance; through the faculty of the nose I perceive fragrances without hindrance; through the faculty of the tongue I discern tastes without hindrance; through the faculty of the body I enter shapes without hindrance; through the faculty of the mind I comprehend knowledge without hindrance. These six faculties, fully adorned, bring all things to completion. The whole luminous true teaching, from beginningless time and from the very first of causes and conditions, has accumulated without limit the luojimian [?] blessing. That blessing is immeasurably weighty, myriads of millions, comparable to the Mountain of the Lord [?]. No comparison can reach it, yet it can be attained. Only then do all good beings come together in the true and real; through this wisdom and light they are illuminated throughout. Advancing through profound understanding, they reach the land of peace and joy, pass beyond that congealed perfection [?], and have a life that is no longer subject to rebirth.

"Simon! Such immeasurable luojimian [?] blessing gives wide relief and benefit beyond conception. Yet when I reflect on myself now, there is truly nothing I have realized. Why? If I said I had realized something, I could not be called unhindered. Therefore I say: without desire, without striving, without virtue, without realization—these four principles do not boast of one's own abilities and are beyond all words. Gentle and lowly, without [?], one quietly exercises great compassion, desiring to bring the countless multitudes of people to complete deliverance. Among all teachings this attains the very highest. Because it attains the highest, it is called the Way of Peace and Joy."

Then Simon rose again, bowed, and praised him, saying: "Great is the Supreme One! Great is the Supreme One! You are able to expound this subtle and supreme Law, so profound and beyond conception. I have not yet fully grasped its meaning; I pray you to instruct me further. Just now the Honored One said: without desire, without striving, without virtue, without realization—these four principles are called the Way of Peace and Joy. I do not understand how, within nothingness, there can be joy."

The One, the Messiah, said: "A fine question, a fine question! Listen carefully and I will explain it to you again. It is only within nothingness that substance can arise; within being, there is never peace and joy. Why is this? Consider an empty mountain: all its trees, with their many branches and scattered leaves, spread out shadow and cast shade. Yet this mountain forest does not seek birds and beasts; all the birds and beasts seek it out of their own accord to roost and gather there. Or consider the great ocean: all its waters are vast and boundless, deep beyond measuring. Yet this ocean does not seek fish and shellfish; all the fish and shellfish dwell in it of their own accord. Living beings who have the right conditions and seek peace and joy are just the same. Simply settle your heart, dwell in stillness, and constantly practice my teaching. Do not seek peace and joy, and peace and joy will come of themselves. That is why within nothingness the things that exist can arise."

The Messiah further said to Simon and the whole great assembly: "What this scripture teaches is divine, wondrous, and hard to conceive. All the saints and sages who have handed down the teachings of the Law have without exception taken this deep and wondrous true teaching as their foundation. It is like creatures with eyes who wish to travel: they must rely on the light of the sun to see far. Simon! This scripture is like that. It can enable those with good hearts, now and in the future, to see the Way of Peace and Joy, and so it is the root of all teachings for ordinary people and saints alike. If there is anyone who hears this scripture expounded and rejoices, draws near to it and makes offerings, reads, recites, receives, and keeps it, know that this person, together with his ancestors and father, has formed good bonds not just for one or two generations, but must have accumulated good roots through generations in the past. Because he can show reverence toward my teaching, he obtains protection through it, and therefore cherishes the desire for this joy. It is like spring rain, which moistens everything: all things that have roots put forth shoots and sprouts, but what has no root never grows. Simon! You and the rest are like this: that you are able to come to me and ask about the supreme Law means that your fathers and ancestors, your relatives and kin over several generations, abounded in goodness, and this has passed on to you."

Simon, reverent and moved with joy, rose again, bowed, and said to the Honored One: "Greatly kind and greatly compassionate Supreme One, you are able in this way to show us love and kindness. You do not reject us for our ignorance, but patiently encourage and guide us. Because of this, not only I but the fathers and mothers of all beings through hundreds of thousands of myriads of generations obtain, not only today, the conditions for peace and joy. But we have long been sunk in darkness and murkiness, and though we wish to advance in practice, we have never been able to arrive. By what means may we make the conditions for gradual progress?"

The One, the Messiah, said: "So it is, so it is; it is truly as you say. Imagine a mountain of treasure, with jade forests and pearl fruits, bright and shining, sweet and fragrant, able to cure hunger and thirst and to heal every illness. There is a sick man who hears of it and thinks of it day and night, his mind never leaving that forest of fruit. But the road is long and the mountain high, his body is frail and his strength weak, and he only accumulates longing in vain without fulfilling his heart's desire. Fortunately he has a close relative, endowed with wisdom and skill, who sets up a ladder for him, leads him, and supports him, so that in the end he obtains what he sought and is rid of his chronic illness. Simon! The hearts of people in times to come will long be entangled in delusion and affliction. They will hear that the fruit of desirelessness is on the mountain of peace and joy, and though they think of advancing in practice, their faith will falter halfway. Fortunately there will be good teachers who act as that close relative, skillfully giving instruction and parables that serve as a ladder, so that all may awaken to the Way and dispel their accumulated delusion. There are ten kinds of contemplation that form the path of gradual practice. What are the ten kinds of contemplation?

"First: contemplate that in the human world the bodily life of flesh gradually grows old and decays, and that none escapes death. It is like an inn where one lodges for a brief while: the beds and bedding provided and the abundant [?] delicacies are none of them one's own, and have nothing to do with one's own affairs. One must leave them in the end; who can stay long?

"Second: contemplate that in the human world one's beloved family and kin must in the end be parted, and it is hard to keep them together. It is like the many leaves that grow on one tree: when wind and frost arrive, the branches wither, and the leaves scatter and fall until none remain.

"Third: contemplate that in the human world high rank, honor, splendor, and prosperity never last forever. It is like the moon at night: its full light shines in every direction, but clouds and mists rise one after another, and it wanes and waxes from the last day of the month to the first. Though it has its brightness, how can one rely on it for long?

"Fourth: contemplate that in the human world those who are overbearing and full of self, though they wish to benefit themselves, end up harming themselves. It is like moths that see a fire at night: they circle and fling themselves into it, thinking it a good thing, not knowing that their lives will end in the flames.

"Fifth: contemplate that in the human world the hoarding of wealth and treasure wearies the spirit and torments the body, and in the end is of no use. It is like a small jar that holds barely a pint: if you ladle water from the rivers and seas and pour it into the jar, once it is full it can take in no more.

"Sixth: contemplate that in the human world indulgence in lust arises from one's own bodily nature and becomes the enemy of that nature. It is like a boring insect born inside a tree: it can injure the tree's nature, eating only its heartwood, until finally the tree withers and rots and gradually breaks and falls.

"Seventh: contemplate that in the human world drinking wine and wanton pleasure bring stupor, confusion, and drunken disorder, so that one cannot tell right from wrong. It is like a clear spring that reflects everything: all things with form are clearly shown in it. But if mud is added, the reflections are lost at once; there is only foulness and murk, and nothing can be seen.

"Eighth: contemplate that in the human world people idle away their days at games and play, wearing out their spirits. It is like a madman whose eyes are dazzled and who sees false visions: he grasps and flails with hands and feet all night without rest, until his sinews and strength are exhausted, and in the end gains nothing.

"Ninth: contemplate that in the human world people practice mixed teachings, concerning themselves only with active striving, and so obstruct and lose what is upright and true. It is like a skilled craftsman who fashions oxen and livestock, adorns and paints them in color until they look real; yet if they are put to work in the fields, they will never bring in a harvest.

"Tenth: contemplate that in the human world people practice good works falsely, seeking only the praise of others and never considering that they deceive themselves. It is like a clam holding a bright pearl: the fisherman breaks it open, takes the pearl, and the clam dies. It can only adorn others and knows nothing of its own suffering.

"Contemplate these ten things and so govern body and mind. When words and deeds accord with each other, there is no fault, and only then can one advance to the four supreme principles. What are the four?

"The first is to be without desire. This means that when the inner heart is stirred by desire and seeks worldly things, it creates the conditions for every evil. It must be subdued, and not allowed to grasp at will. Why? It is like the root of a plant hidden underground: if it is damaged within, nothing can be seen from outside, yet you will see the sprouts and crops wither and droop. People are the same. When there is desire in the heart, it cannot be seen from outside, yet the four limbs and seven openings all lack good vital energy; every evil increases, and the cause of peace and joy is cut off. Therefore, in the inner heart, practice the principle of desirelessness.

"The second is to be without striving. This means that when the outward body acts and builds things that are not the principle of true life, it pursues empty and false conditions. These must be cast aside and not drawn near. Why? It is like boarding a ship and setting out on the great sea: it is tossed by the wind and carried by the waves, and while one fears sinking, there is no peace or rest. People are the same. When the outward body strives and labors at worldly things, it is intent only on gain and never considers the toil, and every good condition is forgotten and abandoned. Therefore, in the outward body, walk the way of non-striving.

"The third is to be without virtue. In all meritorious deeds, take no pleasure in fame. Always practice great kindness and save all kinds of beings far and wide, yet never speak of it as one's own ability. Why? It is like the great earth, which gives birth to and nourishes all things, each according to its nature and all as suits them; its benefits cannot be fully told in words. People are the same. Holding to the supreme Law and practicing the cause of the luminous teaching, they save living beings as well and share peace and joy with them, yet make no claim at all for this wondrous work. This is called being without virtue.

"The fourth is to be without realization. In all true realization, one has no awareness of it, forgets and lays aside right and wrong, and makes gain and loss alike. Though one is said to be free, one is as remote as empty space. Why? It is like a bright mirror that reflects everything: blue, yellow, and every mixture of color, long and short and every shape—it can show them all clearly, yet does not know how it does so. People are the same. Awakening to the nature of the true Way and gaining a heart of peace and joy, they see all conditions everywhere and understand them all, yet of that awareness and understanding they forget everything, leaving nothing behind. This is called being without realization."

The Messiah further said: "If someone is about to go into battle, he must rely on armor and weapons to protect his body; when his armor and weapons are strong, he does not fear his enemies. Just so, this supreme text of the luminous teaching can defend living beings against the bandits of affliction, as armor and weapons protect the body. If someone is about to cross the great sea, he must rely on a ship to get through the wind and waves; when the ship is sound, the far shore can be reached. Just so, this supreme text of the luminous teaching can carry living beings across the sea of birth and death to the shore of the Way, to the precious fragrance [?] of peace and joy. If at some time a plague breaks out, and the sick are many and the dead are many as well, and if they perceive the wondrous scent of the precious incense that restores souls, then the dead return to life and illness and suffering vanish. Just so, this supreme text of the luminous teaching can restore living beings to the life of true wisdom, and all their sins and sufferings are wiped away. If there are men or women who follow my words, diligently practice the supreme Law, and reflect on it day and night, leaving all defilement, so that their true nature is pure, clear, perfect, and bright, know that such people will in the end be set free. Know, then, that the benefits produced by this scripture could be told by all the heavens without ever exhausting its true limit. If people believe in it and love it and practice it even a little, they need not fear any calamity on the path of light, nor meet with any disaster on the path of darkness, and in other lands and strange places they will always have peace and joy—how much more those who practice it wholeheartedly! You my disciples and all who hear, scatter throughout the world and spread this scripture of mine; it can keep the realms of kings in peace and safety. It is like a great fire on a high mountain, which all the people of the country cannot fail to see. A king in his honor is like that high mountain; the benefit of my scripture is like that great fire. If it is put into practice, it will be like light, shining forth of its own accord."

Simon rose again to ask for further instruction. The Messiah said: "Stop, stop; say no more. It is like a good well, whose water is never exhausted; but someone just recovering from illness must not drink too much, lest the water not be digested and bring on a relapse. You are the same. Your good nature has only just begun to stir; hearing too much would lead to doubt. I may not say more."
When the whole great assembly had heard these words, they received them with reverence and joy, bowed, withdrew, and put them into practice.
